sources.text: Since many people confuse congestion control and flow control, we restate the difference. Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact.

Fifth, because the transmitting side of a directly connected link cannot send any faster than the bandwidth of the link allows, and only one host is pumping data into the link, it is not possible to unknowingly congest the link. Said another way, the load on the link is visible in the form of a queue of packets at the sender. In contrast, the sending side of a TCP connection has no idea what links will be traversed to reach the destination. For example, the sending machine might be directly connected to a relatively fast Ethernet—and capable of sending data at a rate of 10 Gbps—but somewhere out in the middle of the network, a 1.5-Mbps link must be traversed. And, to make matters worse, data being generated by many different sources might be trying to traverse this same slow link. This leads to the problem of network congestion. Discussion of this topic is delayed until the next chapter.

It is now possible to understand how a slow receiving process ultimately stops a fast sending process. First, the receive buffer fills up, which means the advertised window shrinks to 0. An advertised window of 0 means that the sending side cannot transmit any data, even though data it has previously sent has been successfully acknowledged. Finally, not being able to transmit any data means that the send buffer fills up, which ultimately causes TCP to block the sending process. As soon as the receiving process starts to read data again, the receive-side TCP is able to open its window back up, which allows the send-side TCP to transmit data out of its buffer. When this data is eventually acknowledged, LastByteAcked is incremented, the buffer space holding this acknowledged data becomes free, and the sending process is unblocked and allowed to proceed.

6.3 TCP Congestion Control

This section describes the predominant example of end-to-end congestion control in use today, which is implemented by TCP. The essential strategy of TCP is to send packets into the network without a reservation and then to react to observable events that occur. TCP assumes only FIFO queuing in the network’s routers, but also works with other queuing strategies.

TCP maintains a new state variable for each connection, called CongestionWindow, which is used by the source to limit how much data it is allowed to have in transit at a given time. The congestion window is congestion control’s counterpart to flow control’s advertised window. TCP is modified such that the maximum number of bytes of unacknowledged data allowed is now the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window. Thus, using the variables defined in the previous chapter, TCP’s effective window is revised as follows:

That is, MaxWindow replaces AdvertisedWindow in the calculation of EffectiveWindow. Thus, a TCP source is allowed to send no faster than the slowest component—the network or the destination host—can accommodate.

In addition to the above features, TCP also implements a highly tuned congestion-control mechanism. The idea of this mechanism is to throttle how fast TCP sends data, not for the sake of keeping the sender from over-running the receiver, but so as to keep the sender from overloading the network. A description of TCP’s congestion-control mechanism is postponed until the next chapter, where we discuss it in the larger context of how network resources are fairly allocated.

Since many people confuse congestion control and flow control, we restate the difference. Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact.

questions.stem:
A TCP sender is connected at a time when the receiver application is slow and the network path contains a bottleneck link shared with many other senders. Use the supplied definitions and variables to reason about which constraint limits transmission in each situation.

Definitions you may use:
1. Flow control prevents senders from over-running the capacity of receivers; congestion control prevents too much data from being injected into the network, causing switches or links to become overloaded.
2. TCP maintains CongestionWindow for congestion control and AdvertisedWindow for flow control.
3. The maximum number of bytes of unacknowledged data allowed is the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window; MaxWindow replaces AdvertisedWindow in the calculation of EffectiveWindow.
4. When the receive buffer fills, the advertised window shrinks to 0, so the sender cannot transmit even if earlier data was acknowledged; when the receiving process reads again, the window opens and the sender can transmit out of its buffer.
5. The sending side of a TCP connection has no idea which links will be traversed, so a fast sender can reach a slow shared link and contribute to network congestion.

Situation A: The receiver has advertised a window of 0 while the network is lightly loaded.
Situation B: The advertised window is large, but the sender has filled the network path to a bottleneck shared by many sources, causing queues to build in routers.


In one or two sentences for each situation, state which control mechanism is the active sending constraint and explain why. Then justify why TCP's effective sending limit uses the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window rather than either one alone.
questions.answer:
Situation A: Flow control is the binding constraint. AdvertisedWindow = 0 makes the maximum unacknowledged data zero, so the sender cannot transmit even though the network may be lightly loaded; this protects the slow receiver from being over-run.

Situation B: Congestion control is the binding constraint. The large advertised window means the receiver is not the limit; the filled bottleneck and queue buildup show the network path is overloaded, so the congestion window is the smaller limit that restricts injection into the network.

Using the minimum: TCP must respect both the destination host and the network at the same time. Because the allowed unacknowledged data is the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window (MaxWindow), the sender is throttled by whichever is smaller, the network or the destination host, so neither receiver over-run nor network overload is neglected.
questions.explanation: Situation A is a receiver-capacity problem: a zero advertised window directly stops transmission despite prior acknowledgments. Situation B is a network-interaction problem: the receiver can accept more, but the path cannot, so the congestion window becomes the smaller limit. Taking the minimum reflects that the sender must not exceed either constraint; it sends no faster than the slowest component can accommodate. These distinctions match the supplied definitions of flow control and congestion control.
questions.difficulty_reason: The learner must apply two related but distinct control concepts to two contrasting concrete scenarios, identify which mechanism is actually binding in each, and justify why the effective window is the minimum rather than either window alone. This requires integrating definitions with the zero-window behavior and the minimum-window rule from the sources, not merely recalling a single definition.

expected_steps: Situation A: identify flow control as the binding constraint because advertised window = 0 stops transmission even if the network is lightly loaded.
Situation B: identify congestion control as the binding constraint because the bottleneck and queues show network overload, not receiver overload.
Justify using the minimum: the sender must respect both receiver capacity and network capacity, so the smaller of the advertised window and congestion window is the safe limit.

questions.stem:
A TCP sender is connected at a time when the receiver application is slow and the network path contains a bottleneck link shared with many other senders. Use the supplied definitions and variables to reason about which constraint limits transmission in each situation.

Definitions you may use:
1. Flow control prevents senders from over-running the capacity of receivers; congestion control prevents too much data from being injected into the network, causing switches or links to become overloaded.
2. TCP maintains CongestionWindow for congestion control and AdvertisedWindow for flow control.
3. The maximum number of bytes of unacknowledged data allowed is the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window; MaxWindow replaces AdvertisedWindow in the calculation of EffectiveWindow.
4. When the receive buffer fills, the advertised window shrinks to 0, so the sender cannot transmit even if earlier data was acknowledged; when the receiving process reads again, the window opens and the sender can transmit out of its buffer.
5. The sending side of a TCP connection has no idea which links will be traversed, so a fast sender can reach a slow shared link and contribute to network congestion.

Situation A: The receiver has advertised a window of 0 while the network is lightly loaded.
Situation B: The advertised window is large, but the sender has filled the network path to a bottleneck shared by many sources, causing queues to build in routers.


In one or two sentences for each situation, state which control mechanism is the active sending constraint and explain why. Then justify why TCP's effective sending limit uses the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window rather than either one alone.
questions.answer:
Situation A: Flow control is the binding constraint. AdvertisedWindow = 0 makes the maximum unacknowledged data zero, so the sender cannot transmit even though the network may be lightly loaded; this protects the slow receiver from being over-run.

Situation B: Congestion control is the binding constraint. The large advertised window means the receiver is not the limit; the filled bottleneck and queue buildup show the network path is overloaded, so the congestion window is the smaller limit that restricts injection into the network.

Using the minimum: TCP must respect both the destination host and the network at the same time. Because the allowed unacknowledged data is the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window (MaxWindow), the sender is throttled by whichever is smaller, the network or the destination host, so neither receiver over-run nor network overload is neglected.
questions.explanation: Situation A is a receiver-capacity problem: a zero advertised window directly stops transmission despite prior acknowledgments. Situation B is a network-interaction problem: the receiver can accept more, but the path cannot, so the congestion window becomes the smaller limit. Taking the minimum reflects that the sender must not exceed either constraint; it sends no faster than the slowest component can accommodate. These distinctions match the supplied definitions of flow control and congestion control.

The following concepts are available from the course material:
- Flow control prevents senders from over-running the capacity of receivers and is an end-to-end issue.
- Congestion control prevents too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded; it concerns how hosts and networks interact.
- TCP maintains a CongestionWindow that limits how much data the source is allowed to have in transit.

Scenario:
A TCP sender S is directly connected to a 10 Gbps Ethernet. The path to receiver R crosses a 1.5-Mbps bottleneck link in the middle of the network. Several other TCP sources also send data across that same 1.5-Mbps link. R runs a slow receiving process, and its receive buffer has filled completely, so R's advertised window is 0. S currently has unacknowledged data in flight that was successfully acknowledged earlier, and S's own send buffer is filling. S's CongestionWindow is currently 64 KB.

For each situation below, state whether the active sending constraint is flow control, congestion control, or the minimum of both, and justify your answer by naming the limiting condition.

1. S is sending to R while R's advertised window is 0.

2. R's receiving process resumes, R advertises a large window, and S's CongestionWindow is still 64 KB while the bottleneck link is heavily loaded by other sources.

3. S is directly connected to a fast Ethernet with no other sources, and a separate TCP connection from a different sender crosses the congested 1.5-Mbps link.

Thus the effective sending rate is bounded by whichever of receiver capacity or network capacity is smaller.

questions.stem:
A TCP sender S transmits a byte stream to a receiver R over a path that may traverse multiple links and routers.

For each situation, identify whether the active sending constraint on S is receiver flow control, network congestion control, neither, or both, and justify your choice by naming the state variable or observable condition that imposes the constraint and explaining what it protects.

1. R's receive buffer is full. R advertises a window of 0 bytes. S has previously sent data that has all been acknowledged.
2. R advertises a large window, but the path from S to R traverses a 1.5-Mbps link that is shared with many other senders. S's congestion window has recently been reduced.
3. S's path to R also crosses a congested 1.5-Mbps link, and S's congestion window is large while R's advertised window is also large. Measurements show that packets from S are being dropped at an intermediate router on that path.

Finally, state whether S is ever allowed to transmit more unacknowledged data than both the congestion window and the advertised window permit, and explain why in terms of the effective window.
questions.answer:
Situation 1 — Receiver flow control: R's advertised window has shrunk to 0, which means S cannot transmit any data even though earlier data was acknowledged; flow control prevents over-running the receiver's capacity.

Situation 2 — Network congestion control: R's advertised window is large, so the receiver is not the bottleneck; the constraint comes from the shared 1.5-Mbps link and S's reduced congestion window, which limits data in transit to avoid overloading switches or links.

Situation 3 — Network congestion control: both the advertised window and congestion window are large, so neither receiver nor window size is the active constraint; the observable packet drops at an intermediate router indicate network congestion, and congestion control is the mechanism that reacts to prevent overloading the network. (Flow control is not active because R is not the limiting factor.)

Final — No. S may send at most the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window. The effective window equals min(congestion window, advertised window), so S is limited by the slowest of the two: the network or the destination host.

Situation 1 is flow control: the source states that when the receive buffer fills, the advertised window shrinks to 0 and the sender cannot transmit any data even though prior data was acknowledged. This protects the receiver, an end-to-end issue.

Situation 2 is congestion control: a large advertised window removes the receiver as the bottleneck, while a shared slow link and reduced congestion window indicate the network is the constraint. Congestion control prevents too much data from being injected into the network.

Situation 3 is congestion control: both windows are large, so the effective window would not limit S by itself; packet drops at a router are the observable event that congestion control reacts to. Flow control is not the active constraint because R is not over-run.

Final: the effective window uses min(congestion window, advertised window), so S cannot exceed either one. This matches the source statement that a TCP source sends no faster than the slowest component—the network or the destination host.

response.answer: The effective send limit is the minimum of the congestion window and the receiver's advertised window: EffectiveWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow). Therefore, S is never allowed to transmit more unacknowledged data than both windows permit; it is limited by whichever of the two is smaller. 1. Receiver flow control is the active constraint. R advertises a window of 0 bytes, so AdvertisedWindow = 0 and the effective window is 0 even though previously sent data has all been acknowledged. This protects R's receive buffer from being over-run by a fast sender. 2. Network congestion control is the active constraint. Although R advertises a large window, the path traverses a 1.5-Mbps shared link and S's congestion window has recently been reduced, so CongestionWindow is the limiting value. This protects the shared network link and routers from being overloaded by too much injected data. 3. Network congestion control is the active constraint. Even with a large advertised window and a large congestion window, packets from S are being dropped at an intermediate router, which is an observable congestion signal. S must reduce or limit its sending in response to the loss/drop condition, protecting the congested link/router resources. In all cases, the effective window is min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow); sending cannot exceed this minimum.

2. R advertises a large window, but the path from S to R traverses a 1.5-Mbps link that is shared with many other senders. S's congestion window has recently been reduced.
3. S's path to R also crosses a congested 1.5-Mbps link, and S's congestion window is large while R's advertised window is also large. Measurements show that packets from S are being dropped at an intermediate router on that path.

Final — No. S may send at most the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window. The effective window equals min(congestion window, advertised window), so S is limited by the slowest of the two: the network or the destination host.

For example, the sending machine might be directly connected to a relatively fast Ethernet—and capable of sending data at a rate of 10 Gbps—but somewhere out in the middle of the network, a 1.5-Mbps link must be traversed. And, to make matters worse, data being generated by many different sources might be trying to traverse this same slow link. This leads to the problem of network congestion. Discussion of this topic is delayed until the next chapter.

It is now possible to understand how a slow receiving process ultimately stops a fast sending process. First, the receive buffer fills up, which means the advertised window shrinks to 0. An advertised window of 0 means that the sending side cannot transmit any data, even though data it has previously sent has been successfully acknowledged. Finally, not being able to transmit any data means that the send buffer fills up, which ultimately causes TCP to block the sending process. As soon as the receiving process starts to read data again, the receive-side TCP is able to open its window back up, which allows the send-side TCP to transmit data out of its buffer. When this data is eventually acknowledged, LastByteAcked is incremented, the buffer space holding this acknowledged data becomes free, and the sending process is unblocked and allowed to proceed.

6.3 TCP Congestion Control

This section describes the predominant example of end-to-end congestion control in use today, which is implemented by TCP. The essential strategy of TCP is to send packets into the network without a reservation and then to react to observable events that occur. TCP assumes only FIFO queuing in the network’s routers, but also works with other queuing strategies.

TCP maintains a new state variable for each connection, called CongestionWindow, which is used by the source to limit how much data it is allowed to have in transit at a given time. The congestion window is congestion control’s counterpart to flow control’s advertised window. TCP is modified such that the maximum number of bytes of unacknowledged data allowed is now the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window. In addition to the above features, TCP also implements a highly tuned congestion-control mechanism. The idea of this mechanism is to throttle how fast TCP sends data, not for the sake of keeping the sender from over-running the receiver, but so as to keep the sender from overloading the network. A description of TCP’s congestion-control mechanism is postponed until the next chapter, where we discuss it in the larger context of how network resources are fairly allocated.

Since many people confuse congestion control and flow control, we restate the difference. Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact.
